To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
happy people show mood-congruent self-esteem effects, whereas sad people show mood-incongruent self-esteem.
mood congruence and inclusion-exclusion effects interact to determine whether recalling either a positive self or a negative self increases or decreases self-esteem.
mood congruence increases self-esteem, and mood incongruency decreases self-esteem.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How do happy and sad people differ in their perceptions of the mood congruence of past and present selves?
how people use their past selves to evaluate their current self and shows that people use the same past selves to increase or decrease self-esteem, depending on the mood they are in at the time.
the role of mood in the inclusion-exclusion of past self-views and the resulting impact on self-esteem.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effect of recalling a positive or a neutral self on self-esteem depends on the chronic mood of the perceiver and that the effect of a negative self on self-esteem is determined by both the chronic mood of perceiver and the mood of the target self.
mood congruence is information, which can either be assimilated or contrasted with current information.

recalling a past self increases self-esteem if the past self is judged to be temporally recent (i.e., mood-congruent), whereas recalling a past self decreases self-esteem if the recalled self is judged to temporally distant (i.e., moods-incongruent).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inclusion-exclusion principle is not only a principle of social judgment, but also a principle of self-judgment.
the inclusion-exclusion of past selves depends on the mood congruency of the past selves with respect to the present self.
mood congruence is information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mood congruence is not always a good thing.
the effects of recalling a positive or a positive self are not fixed and invariant but rather depend on the current state of the self.
the impact of recalling a positive or a neutral self on self-esteem depends on how the recalled self is perceived in the context of the current self.
